# Summary

## Data cleaning

At this point, I've cleaned both YT and BC data to:

1\) remove points that are not geographically feasible (in Germany, the ocean, etc)

2\) remove any pre-/post-deployment points

3\) remove first week of data (capture effect)

4\) remove low quality steps: DOP \< 10 (if recorded)

5\) remove duplicate points

6\) remove unreasonably fast steps (preliminary)

7\) remove fast round trips

8\) remove defunct clusters (post death/fall off)

9\) remove individuals with less than 3 points

Now, we have a "clean" data set.

## Exploring the data

```{r}

#| label: setup

#| include: false

require('data.table')

require('amt')

require('dplyr')

require('tidyr')

require('sf')

require('terra')

require('ggplot2')

require('tidyterra')

### Input data ----

raw <- file.path('data','raw')

derived <- file.path('data','derived')

#canada <- file.path('~/Dropbox', 'ActiveDocs', 'Git-local', 'Can_GIS_layers')

canada <- file.path('C:','Users', 'julie', 'Dropbox', 'ActiveDocs', 'Git-local', 'Can_GIS_layers')

dat <- readRDS(file.path(derived, 'clean_NMC.RDS'))

crs <- st_crs(3154)

canPoly <- vect(file.path(canada, 'CanadaPoly', 'lpr_000b16a_e.shp'))

```

Now we're going to explore the clean data.

```{r}

#| echo: true

sArea <- vect(file.path(derived, 'prepped', 'clean_NMC_20kmBuff.shp'))

nmc.juris <- subset(canPoly, canPoly$PREABBR %in% c('B.C.', 'Y.T.'))

nmc.juris <- project(nmc.juris, sArea)

ggplot(nmc.juris) +

  geom_spatvector(fill = NA) +

  geom_spatvector(data = sArea, fill = 'blueviolet') +

  ggtitle('Buffered clean locations') +

  theme_bw() +

  theme(plot.title=element_text(size=12,hjust = 0.05),axis.title = element_blank()) +

  theme_void() +

  coord_sf(crs = crs)

```

Clearly, still not perfectly clean, but it's a good starting point.

At this point, there are `r nrow(dat)` in our cleaned data set.

### Fix rates

Now we're going to explore what the range of fix rates looks like across the whole data set

```{r}

#| echo: false

fixrate.clean <- dat %>% make_track(x_,y_, t_, crs = crs, all_cols = T) %>% 

  nest(data = -"id") %>% 

  mutate(sr = lapply(data, summarize_sampling_rate)) %>%

  dplyr::select(id, sr) %>% unnest(cols = c(sr))

```

c

```{r}

#| echo: false

quantile(fixrate.clean$mean)

```

Quantiles of median fix rates by individual

```{r}

#| echo: false

# quantile of median fix rates by individual

quantile(fixrate.clean$median)

```

Mean of the median fix rates by individual

```{r}

#| echo: false

mean(fixrate.clean$median)

```

### Steps

#### 8 hour fix rate

Let's explore the all the step regardless of fix rate

```{r}

#| echo: false

steps <- 

  dat %>% 

  nest(data = -id) %>% 

  mutate(track = map(data, ~ mk_track(., x_, y_, t_, crs= crs)))

step.lengths <- unlist(map(steps$track, step_lengths))

hist(step.lengths, ylim = c(0, 1000), main="Histogram of step lengths", xlab="Step lengths")

```

The median of median fix rates was 8 hours, so let's check out resampling to this fix rate

```{r}

#| echo: false

trk.fr <- dat |> 

  make_track(x_, y_, t_, all_cols = T, crs = crs) |> 

  nest(data = -"id") |> 

  mutate(resamp = map(data, function(x) 

    x |> track_resample(rate = hours(8), tolerance = minutes(90))))

# trk.fr %>% unnest(steps) %>%

#   inspect(cluster=FALSE)

trk.fr %>% unnest(resamp) %>%

  plot(main = "8 hour fix rate")

```

Step length distribution

```{r}

#| echo: false

steps.fr <- trk.fr |> mutate(steps = map(resamp, function(x)

  x |> steps_by_burst()))

steps.fr |> select(id,  steps)|>

  unnest(cols = steps)|> 

  ggplot(aes(sl_)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.4)

```

This is a typical distribution, though it looks like there are still a few unnaturally long steps. So let's check the quantiles.

```{r}

#| echo: false

steps.id <- steps.fr |> select(id,  steps)|>

  unnest(cols = steps)

quantile(steps.id$sl_)

```

At the extremes:

```{r}

#| echo: false

quantile(steps.id$sl_, probs = c(0.9, 0.95, 0.99))

```

So, looks like we could filter out the top 99% of steps if we need to remove the unrealistically long 34 km step taken in within 8 hours...

Now, lets check out the turn angles

```{r}

#| echo: false

#| warning: false

steps.fr |> select(id,  steps)|>

  unnest(cols = steps)|> 

  ggplot(aes(ta_)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.4)

```

That's a nice looking von Mises distribution, so looks good.

However, this fix rate leads to us only having `r nrow(steps.id)` out of the original `r nrow(dat)` observations. Not terrible, but let's check another fix rate.

#### 13 hour fix rate

The 75% quantile of median fix rates was 13 hours, so we'll try that next.

```{r}

#| echo: false

trk.fr13 <- dat |> 

  make_track(x_, y_, t_, all_cols = T, crs = crs) |> 

  nest(data = -"id") |> 

  mutate(resamp = map(data, function(x) 

    x |> track_resample(rate = hours(13), tolerance = minutes(90))))

# trk.fr %>% unnest(steps) %>%

#   inspect(cluster=FALSE)

trk.fr13 %>% unnest(resamp) %>%

  plot(main = "13 hour fix rate")

```

Let's check the step length distribution:

```{r}

#| echo: false

steps.fr13 <- trk.fr13 |> mutate(steps = map(resamp, function(x)

  x |> steps_by_burst()))

steps.fr13 |> select(id,  steps)|>

  unnest(cols = steps)|> 

  ggplot(aes(sl_)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.4)

```

Again, this looks good but has some unrealistically long step lengths, so let's explore deeper.

```{r}

#| echo: false

steps.id13 <- steps.fr13 |> select(id,  steps)|>

  unnest(cols = steps)

quantile(steps.id13$sl_)

```

And, at the extremes:

```{r}

#| echo: false

quantile(steps.id13$sl_, probs = c(0.9, 0.95, 0.99))

```

Again, looks like we could filter out the top 99% of steps if we need to remove the unrealistically long 66 km step taken in within 13 hours...

Let's check the turn angles:

```{r}

#| echo: false

#| warning: false

steps.fr13 |> select(id,  steps)|>

  unnest(cols = steps)|> 

  ggplot(aes(ta_)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.4)

```

This also looks good.

Now, this fix rate leads to us having `r nrow(steps.id13)` out of the original `r nrow(dat)` observations. So, this is better than the `r nrow(steps.id)` observations at the 8 hour fix rate.

#### 25 hour fix rate

Let's try a 25 hour fix rate to see if we can get more data. This comes with the trade off of our inferences from movement parameters being very coarse.

```{r}

#| echo: false

trk.fr25 <- dat |> 

  make_track(x_, y_, t_, all_cols = T, crs = crs) |> 

  nest(data = -"id") |> 

  mutate(resamp = map(data, function(x) 

    x |> track_resample(rate = hours(25), tolerance = minutes(120))))

# trk.fr %>% unnest(steps) %>%

#   inspect(cluster=FALSE)

trk.fr25 %>% unnest(resamp) %>%

  plot(main = "25 hour fix rate")

```

Let's check the step length distribution:

```{r}

#| echo: false

steps.fr25 <- trk.fr25 |> mutate(steps = map(resamp, function(x)

  x |> steps_by_burst()))

steps.fr25 |> select(id,  steps)|>

  unnest(cols = steps)|> 

  ggplot(aes(sl_)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.4)

```

Again, this looks good. Let's explore deeper.

```{r}

#| echo: false

steps.id25 <- steps.fr25 |> select(id,  steps)|>

  unnest(cols = steps)

quantile(steps.id25$sl_)

```

And, at the extremes:

```{r}

#| echo: false

quantile(steps.id25$sl_, probs = c(0.9, 0.95, 0.99))

```

Again, looks like we could filter out the top 99% of steps if we needed. Is 80 km unrealistically long in 25 hours? Probably?

Let's check the turn angles:

```{r}

#| echo: false

#| warning: false

steps.fr25 |> select(id,  steps)|>

  unnest(cols = steps)|> 

  ggplot(aes(ta_)) + geom_density(alpha = 0.4)

```

That's a nice looking von Mises distribution, so looks good.

Now, this fix rate leads to us having `r nrow(steps.id25)` out of the original `r nrow(dat)` observations. So, this is better than the `r nrow(steps.id)` observations at the 8 hour fix rate and less than the `r nrow(steps.id13)` observations at the 13 hour fix rate. The 13 hour fix rate is probably our sweet spot
